extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism and mass communication; journalism educators and newsroom managers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative dimensions for how individual journalists' demographics, careers, education, and organizational practices influence news content and newsroom practice. Includes standards for recruitment, education, assignment practices, and empirical assessment of demographic effects on reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-representative hiring goals (ASNE Year 2000 goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should increase the percentage of minorities in their employ to better reflect their community; ASNE set goals for newspapers that are behind to increase minority employment by 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure newsroom minority percentages against community demographics (example: Cleveland Plain Dealer had 12% minorities vs 25% in community). Note that newspapers in smaller-minority communities are likeliest to meet numerical goals. Historical trend (since 1978) showed minority population growing faster than minority employment, implying newspapers could fall further behind if trends continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, targeted recruiting practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should pursue vigorous and targeted recruiting (including national recruitment) to increase minority hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Merced Sun-Star increased from one minority journalist to 20% after a vigorous recruiting campaign; Seattle Times rose from 4% to 21.1% by recruiting nationally and engaging with professional associations (NABJ and similar groups). Effective tools include national searches and active participation in journalist associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of professional associations for recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in organizations representing minority journalists helps recruit diverse staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Seattle Times' success was attributed to active involvement in the National Association for Black Journalists and associations for Asian, Hispanic, and Native Americans. NAHJ surveys showed incremental hires (1992), though increases may be small or 'insignificant' per leaders' assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of sexual orientation in anti-bias policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should consider sexual orientation as a dimension for anti-bias or diversity policy inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some major organizations (Time Warner, Dow Jones, Knight-Ridder, Reuters) include sexual orientation, but most newspapers did not include it (Rosenkrantz, 1992). Creating groups like the National Lesbian and Gay Journalists Association (NLGJA) (job fairs, chapters) supports recruitment and professional development for gay and lesbian journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of reporters' right to disclose sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should avoid punitive actions against journalists who reveal sexual orientation in relation to their reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Juan Palomo (Houston Post) revealed he was gay in a column; editors ordered removal and he was fired when story surfaced elsewhere, though later rehired with reduced visibility. Contrast with Deb Price, who became first syndicated columnist focusing on gay/lesbian issues. Anti-reprisal policies and inclusive assignment practices are implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of managerial dynamics for minority journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion of minority journalists into management creates unique interpersonal and expectation challenges that management must recognize and manage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas Greer's observation: black managers face special problems supervising black staff, including expectations that black staff either be held to higher standards or have lowered expectations. Managers must be aware of these dynamics to avoid paternalistic or biased supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pigeonholing minority journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should not confine minority journalists to minority stories nor deprive them of lead roles on major coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: After LA riots, minority reporters were assigned but then undervalued and denied lead stories; Spike Lee's request for African-American interviewers was refused by LA Times, illustrating tensions between assignment decisions and opportunities. Assignments should balance sensitivity/insight with equal opportunity for major roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to reporters' dual loyalties/emotional burdens on certain beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should recognize that reporters who share identity or proximity to a story (racial/ethnic/sexual orientation) may experience conflict between objectivity expectations and lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidmel Estes-Sumpter's quote about living in two worlds during Rodney King riots: reporters asked to be objective while personally experiencing the rage. Newsrooms should acknowledge these tensions rather than assume lack of professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of representativeness versus elite recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether journalists represent the 'average American' or an elite segment and how that origin affects news priorities and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies differ: Weaver & Wilhoit find journalists come from 'established and dominant cultural groups'; Lichter et al. find elite-media journalists are modern eastern urbanites. Choice of who is studied affects conclusions; recruitment patterns (education, family background) influence the profession's social composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of journalists' age and turnover in staffing policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that journalism has high turnover and a younger workforce, with implications for experience, institutional memory, and beat coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Median age lower than general workforce; more than half under 35. Low pay/benefits drive exits; many leave between 30-45 and those with more education/experience often leave. TV may hire even younger people. Staffing plans should account for career-stage effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for specialty beat expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide for older, better-educated specialty reporters (e.g., science) and value subject-matter expertise for technical beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science writers typically older and better educated; substantive knowledge is essential to translate technical reports for lay audiences (anecdote of photographer misinterpreting nuclear scientists). Newsrooms should invest in expertise or training for complex beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of continuing education targeted to newsroom needs
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should offer continuing education in ethics, science, economics, law, and international affairs to prepare journalists for complex reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1990 survey shows journalists most interested in continuing education in these areas. Some newspapers (e.g., Tampa Tribune) hire select graduates and train them intensively in law, writing, editing, and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between liberal arts depth and vocational skills in journalism education
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism education should strike a balance between broad liberal arts grounding and job-ready technical skills; institutions differ on emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate: some professionals prefer liberal arts with research/theory/critical thinking; others want technical, skills-oriented programs. Accrediting Council guideline historically ~25% in journalism courses and 75% liberal arts. Some schools have wanted to require more in-major credits to meet modern demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement of double majors or subject depth for reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be encouraged to take double majors (e.g., business + journalism) to gain depth in topic areas employers increasingly demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth in subject areas (national security, science, etc.) gives graduates an advantage. Editors sometimes prefer 'tradecraft' skills, but specialized knowledge can set reporters apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical evaluation of journalism textbooks' orientation (insider vs outsider)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether curriculum materials socialize students to be media 'insiders' (teach how to succeed within industry) or 'outsiders' (encourage critical analysis of mass media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoemaker's review: textbooks either socialize students to be insiders or teach them to critique social institutions. Faculty choice of textbooks reflects and shapes students' orientation toward the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty professional experience and scholarly/industry engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty credentials should include professional media experience; faculty reading habits (industry vs scholarly) influence what students learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1987 survey: 98% of full-time mass communication faculty have professional media experience (avg 9 years). Variation exists: 40% keep up with both academic and industry knowledge, ~30% read only industry publications, ~20% only scholarly journals, ~10% neither—this shapes curricular emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational routines and constraints moderate individual demographic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual journalists differ demographically, organizational routines and constraints may limit the impact of those differences on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaver & Wilhoit argue demographic effects are probably minor given strong routines. The question of how much demographics change content is empirical—some studies find differences (e.g., female publishers' coverage of ERA), others show individual variability among journalists of same demographic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simplistic assumptions about objectivity based on identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not assume that reporters' demographic characteristics (gender, race, sexuality) inherently affect objectivity on related beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions like 'Should women be allowed to cover abortion?' expose biased assumptions; analogous questions about men covering sports or war are not asked. Both male and female, heterosexual and gay reporters should be judged by professional standards, not identity-based presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor newsroom culture and interpersonal behavior as part of diversity efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in gender and minority representation should be accompanied by attention to cultural norms, jokes, harassment, and team dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase in women editors reportedly reduced sexist behavior and made newsrooms more collaborative. However, 'gender politics of the unwelcome kind' still pervades some newsrooms; incidents of overt harassment can lead to legal action and negotiated settlements with commitments to improved assignments and hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track job satisfaction and its demographic patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure job satisfaction over time and across demographic groups to understand retention and morale issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys show declining job satisfaction from 1971 to 1992, with African-American and Asian-American journalists least likely to report being 'very satisfied'. Low organizational pride (doing an outstanding job informing public) also declined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the tradeoff between 'tradecraft' generalists and subject specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and educators must weigh the value of general reporting skills ('jacks of all trades') against the need for subject-specific expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some editors prefer generalist tradecraft believing it enables coverage of any event; others argue for deeper expertise. Richard Burt's critique notes skepticism toward colleagues with special expertise as being 'co-opted', which can discourage specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure resource adequacy in journalism programs to match student demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic programs should align enrollment with faculty/resources and up-to-date equipment to provide quality training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget cuts and high demand have left some programs understaffed and with outdated equipment, forcing some schools to teach more basic skills (e.g., grammar) than desired. Programs that restrict enrollment and select strongest applicants better match resources to demand.
